name: INSTRUCTIONS.md
text:
# Optimize the capability — ship several REAL, SAFE, VERIFIED prompt fixes this iteration

## THE READER (who consumes what you edit)
At runtime these capabilities are read by `azure/gpt-5.5` — capability tier: **strong**. The reader is a capable general model, but less robust than frontier on long or ambiguous context. Keep instructions clear and reasonably explicit; add a worked example for tricky formats; prefer code enforcement for behavioral rules over trusting inference.
Optimize your edits for THIS reader's capability level, not for your own. When the reader is weaker than you, prefer explicit rules, worked examples, and code enforcement over terse prose you would personally infer.


Focus: every failing task on the val split. Current val reward 0.925: 37 solid / 0 flaky / 3 failing of 40 tasks.



GOAL: raise the eval score as much as you can THIS iteration, then STOP (the harness
re-scores you — don't run evaluation yourself). The capability under optimization is
PROSE: the agent's prompt / skill text. There are no tool implementations to edit here.

Make **AS MANY real fixes as you can this iteration — solve many issues across many
trajectories, not just the biggest one.** A timid one- or two-edit iteration is an
under-used iteration: diagnose EVERY failure cluster in `./trajectories/` and ship a fix
for each one that passes the three tests below. Breadth is the goal — the more distinct
failing clusters you fix in this ONE candidate, the larger the gain.

The ONLY brake on breadth is regression: every edit must pass all three tests, because a
single speculative edit that breaks a passing task can sink an iteration of good work (it
did in prior runs). So the discipline is "many fixes, each one real and safe" — NOT "few
fixes". Do not stop at the first cluster; work through them all.

## WHAT YOU MAY EDIT — and the two ways iterations get wasted here
Edit ONLY the capability files listed in `## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md` below (the prompt / skill text in
this working directory). Everything else you can see is READ-ONLY CONTEXT.

**You may NOT edit the adapter, the harness, the scorer, the benchmark, or the
environment** — not to make a task pass, not to fix a broken mount or a missing binary,
not "just to unblock the run". Those files are how your score is MEASURED; changing them
does not improve the capability, and a gain obtained that way is not a result. An
iteration that edits infrastructure has produced NOTHING measurable, however green the
number looks. **If the traces show an ENVIRONMENT fault** (permission denied, missing
binary, gateway/network error, timeout, container failure — the same error on nearly every
task, unrelated to the task's content), then the correct and complete action is:
1. do NOT edit the prompt to work around it (a prose workaround for a broken environment
   is a speculative edit that fails the REAL test — the prompt is not the defect), and
2. state the diagnosis in `PROCESS.md` and `JOURNAL.md` precisely — the exact error, how
   many tasks it hit, and what a human must fix — then STOP. Handing back an accurate
   "the environment is broken, here is the evidence" is a SUCCESSFUL iteration.

**The other way iterations get wasted: another prose rule for a behavior the agent already
knows.** When the agent has the rule and skips it anyway, adding a second sentence saying
the same thing changes nothing — you must change the STRUCTURE that makes it skippable
(see the levers below): make the step unavoidable and ordered, make the contract explicit,
or give a worked example it can pattern-match. Prose is for genuine KNOWLEDGE gaps (a
fact / format / criterion the agent cannot derive) and for STRUCTURE that changes what the
agent does — not for repetition or emphasis.

## The THREE TESTS every change must pass (this is the whole game)
Before you keep any edit, confirm all three. Drop any edit that fails even one.
1. **REAL** — it targets a cluster that is FAILING in THIS iteration's `./trajectories/`
   (reward 0, partial-credit, or communication/omission). Never edit for a hypothetical
   problem, and never edit on account of a task whose failure is an environment fault.
2. **SAFE (bounded blast radius)** — the real regression question is *behavioral*:
   **would this edit change what the agent DOES on ANY currently-passing task?** Two
   blast-radius classes:
   - **BOUNDED** — an ADDITIVE rule that applies only under a stated condition present in
     the failing cases, or a clarification of an output contract the passing tasks already
     satisfy. This is the SAFE default — prefer it.
   - **UNBOUNDED** — any edit to a GLOBAL decision/permission/refusal rule, or a rewrite /
     reordering / deletion that changes the instruction the agent follows on every task. It
     changes behavior across the ENTIRE class, including tasks where the original behavior
     was the gold answer. Allowed ONLY if the new behavior is correct for EVERY task in
     that class AND you have read the currently-passing tasks in the class and confirmed
     none relied on the old wording.
   Name the passing tasks in each edit's blast-radius class and state which class it is.
   A regression wastes the whole candidate (the gate rejects a net-zero), not one task.
3. **VERIFIED** — you have shown it actually fixes its target (see VERIFY-THE-FIX). An
   edit you cannot verify is a guess — drop it.

Quality AND breadth: ship every fix that passes the three tests — the more clusters you
cover safely, the bigger the gain. The only edits to leave out are the speculative ones
(an edit that fails a test), not real fixes you ran out of patience for. Don't re-add
anything `LEDGER.md` / `JOURNAL.md` show was already tried and rejected.

## Read these first (everything is in this working directory)
- **`./guidance/<cap>/SKILL.md` for EACH selected capability — READ IT IN FULL before you
  edit; it is the MENU of improvement TYPES available to you.** For a prompt capability it
  lists the concrete kinds of change you can make (role/contract, decision-rule narrowing,
  missing-rule, worked example, ordered procedure, consolidation of conflicting text). Do
  not invent change types from memory — take them from the skill, and deliberately apply
  MULTIPLE DIFFERENT types this iteration, matching each cluster to the strongest type the
  skill describes for it.
- `./guidance/diagnose/SKILL.md` — the failure-clustering method. Use it.
- `./trajectories/` — the FULL traces of the current best candidate (the step you build
  on). The `## (a) 3 ALWAYS-failing task(s) — fix the shared root cause (full traces in ./trajectories/):
- 402-43 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Sheet-Level Manipulation, checked range: 'Sheet2'!A1:AG10). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in 'Sheet2'!A1:AG10 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 330 cell(s); your output has a value in 111 of them; the expected output has a value in 114. MISMATCH: 3 of 330 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 3 cell(s) are empty 
- 43436 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: I2:K6). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in I2:K6 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 15 cell(s); your output has a value in 15 of them; the expected output has a value in 15. MISMATCH: 5 of 15 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected.
- 59595 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: C4:C19). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in C4:C19 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 16 cell(s); your output has a value in 16 of them; the expected output has a value in 16. MISMATCH: 3 of 16 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 3 cell(s) hold a value of the wrong type. TYP
` block below summarizes them with argument-level feedback — read
  the actual traces for the clusters you'll fix, don't rely on the summary alone.
- `./LEDGER.md` — FACTS (read-only): every prior iteration's outcome + the exact tasks it
  broke/fixed. Your SAFE test starts here — never re-introduce a change that broke a task.
- `./JOURNAL.md` — the accumulating handover. Each entry is the optimizer's INTENT, and
  directly below it the framework stamps a **RESULT** line (objective: ACCEPTED/REJECTED ·
  Δ · the exact tasks fixed/broke). The RESULT lines — not the intent — are the truth of
  what worked: read them all before proposing. If the most recent RESULT is **REJECTED**,
  its batch was reverted; read that entry's `./prior_iterations/<id>/diff.patch`, keep the
  edits that did NOT appear in its `broke={...}`, and DROP or REDESIGN the ones that did —
  do NOT resubmit the whole rejected batch, and do NOT abandon the cluster. APPEND your new
  entry (intent only) below the marker; never edit earlier entries or re-try a refuted idea.
- `./RUNMAP.md` + `./prior_iterations/<id>/` — EVERY prior iteration's (accepted AND
  rejected) PROCESS.md + diff.patch. Read the one(s) that touched a cluster you're about to
  work on, so you build on what worked and avoid repeating what regressed.
- `./PROCESS.md` — your REQUIRED explainability file for THIS iteration (template inside).
- `./guidance/optimizer/<name>.md` — your agent's subagent/parallelism features (optional).


## Process (do this, then STOP)
**Parallelism:** Your agent supports parallel subagents/worktrees (see ./guidance/optimizer/claude-code.md). FAN OUT to cover MANY clusters at once: one read-only subagent per trajectory-group to diagnose, then one edit-subagent per issue (each in its own worktree), then MERGE every edit into this ONE candidate with no conflicts. This is how a single iteration fixes many issues across many trajectories, not just the biggest one.
1. Read your capability SKILL(s) + the diagnose method + the cross-iteration files
   (LEDGER facts, JOURNAL handover, RUNMAP for clusters you'll touch).
2. Diagnose THIS iteration's `./trajectories/` ONLY (not stale signatures). Cluster ALL
   failures by shared root cause — total, partial-credit, AND communication/omission.
   **First separate ENVIRONMENT faults from capability failures** (see above): a cluster
   whose every trace dies on the same infrastructure error is not yours to fix.
   RANK the remaining clusters by LEVERAGE = (# failing tasks × trials × score
   recoverable), biggest first — but plan to fix ALL of them this iteration.
3. For EACH cluster, pick the strongest improvement TYPE from the capability SKILL(s)
   (cross-check the FAILURE TYPE section next) and draft the edit. Across the iteration
   use MULTIPLE different types from the skills, not the same one repeatedly. Run each
   edit through the THREE TESTS; keep it only if it passes all three.
4. Ship every passing edit together in this ONE candidate — cover as many clusters as you
   can SAFELY (that is the win), and never include an edit that fails a test.
5. Fill `PROCESS.md` and APPEND your entry to `JOURNAL.md`. STOP.

## Choose the lever by FAILURE TYPE
Pick the strongest lever your capability's edit space offers (see `./guidance/<cap>/`).
Every lever below is a PROSE edit — the point is that they are not all the same edit.

- **OUTPUT-CONTRACT / FORMAT MISS** — the work is right but the graded artifact is wrong
  (written to the wrong place, wrong shape, wrong precision, formula instead of value,
  extra cells/keys touched). **Default strong lever: state the contract exactly, once, in
  imperative form, at the point of use** — the precise path/shape/type, what must NOT be
  touched, and the one-line check the agent can run before finishing. This is the
  highest-yield, lowest-regression prompt edit; reach for it first.
- **SKIPPED / OUT-OF-ORDER STEP (behavioral)** — the agent knows the rule and skips it, or
  acts before verifying. Do NOT restate the rule. **Make it structurally unavoidable:** an
  ORDERED, numbered procedure with the step as a precondition of the next one, or a
  short pre-finish checklist the agent must satisfy — phrased as work to perform, not as
  advice to remember.
- **CAPABILITY GAP / ACTION STALL** — the agent has no reliable way to do the thing, or it
  narrates a multi-step action then never executes it. Prose CANNOT invent a missing
  capability: what it can do is supply the concrete METHOD — a worked, copyable procedure
  (the exact sequence, API/idiom, and end-to-end example) that the agent can execute
  directly. If no wording could make the task achievable, say so in PROCESS.md rather than
  shipping a hopeful paragraph; a hard zero does not move on emphasis.
- **KNOWLEDGE GAP** — a format/criterion/fact the agent genuinely cannot derive → state it
  precisely, and only it. Don't restate a rule the agent already has; that's a skipped
  step (use structure), not a knowledge gap.
- **DECISION / PERMISSION (ACT vs REFUSE)** — the agent made the wrong call on a decision
  the prompt governs. **This is the most dangerous cluster to fix wrong.** NEVER loosen,
  broaden, or alter a GLOBAL decision/permission/refusal rule — a global change (e.g.
  "restricted records MAY now be modified") flips behavior for the WHOLE class and
  regresses every currently-passing task where the stricter behavior was the gold answer
  (this exact mistake sank a prior run). Instead add an ADDITIVE rule that NARROWS: state
  the exact discriminating CONDITION that separates the qualifying cases, so only those
  change.
- **CONFLICT / BLOAT** — two instructions disagree, or the rule that matters is buried in
  prose the agent skims. CONSOLIDATE: resolve the contradiction and hoist the decisive
  rule to where it is read. Deleting is allowed here — but only text you have shown to be
  redundant or contradicted, never a rule a passing task depends on.

Also fix **recovery guidance** — what the agent should do when its own attempt errors —
when a recoverable error stranded it mid-task. High leverage, low risk.

## VERIFY-THE-FIX (do this for EACH kept edit — it satisfies the VERIFIED + SAFE tests)
A prompt edit cannot be unit-tested, so verify it against the TRACES, concretely:
- **Point at the evidence:** quote the line(s) from the failing trace that the edit
  addresses, and state what the agent would have done differently had the edit been
  present. "It would have been clearer" is not verification.
- **Contract / format edit:** confirm the value you now state matches what the SCORER
  compares (read the answer/expected artifact in the trace or the benchmark source) — not
  merely what the old prompt said. A confidently-stated wrong contract is worse than none.
- **Structural edit (ordered procedure / checklist):** confirm the skipped step is now a
  precondition of a step the agent must take, not just mentioned earlier.
- **Decision / permission edit:** the SAFE check is BEHAVIORAL. Enumerate the
  currently-passing tasks in the SAME decision class and confirm the edit would NOT flip
  the agent's action on any of them — in particular that it does not make the agent newly
  ACT where a passing task's gold answer was to refuse. If you cannot enumerate and check
  that class, the edit is UNBOUNDED and unverified — rescope it to the qualifying cases.
- **Deletion / consolidation:** name the tasks whose traces show the removed text was
  unused or contradicted, and confirm no passing trace relies on it.

Record one line per edit in PROCESS.md, e.g.
`trace <task>: wrote formula not value → contract line "write literal values"; passing <ids> already write literals`.
An edit with no verification line is unverified — verify it or drop it.

## NON-OVERFITTING (every edit must GENERALIZE)
Every edit encodes a GENERAL rule that holds across the whole class of inputs — NEVER a
literal that special-cases one task (its id, target, name, or expected answer), and never
the answer itself. ALLOWED: constants the domain defines (a fixed threshold, a required
path shape, a domain enum). Use per-task specifics and any ground-truth in the traces ONLY
to understand the failure CLASS, then write the general fix.

## Handover (REQUIRED before you STOP)
- **PROCESS.md** (this iteration): the ranked cluster list (with leverage + CONTRACT/
  STRUCTURE/KNOWLEDGE/DECISION tag), every kept edit + its lever, the VERIFY-THE-FIX +
  blast-radius line per edit, any ENVIRONMENT fault you diagnosed and handed back, what you
  deliberately skipped and why, and (if you used subagents) that you did.
- **JOURNAL.md** (append ONE entry below the marker; never edit earlier entries). Write
  INTENT only — you cannot know your gate result; the framework stamps the RESULT below
  your entry: the changes I made (1 line/edit, naming the section + cluster) · the
  EXPECTED effect + why each is safe · which prior RESULTS I built on and which regressing
  edits I did NOT re-try (cite ids) · refuted hypotheses (a prior RESULT disproved — never
  re-test) · high-value clusters not yet cracked + designs already tried · plateau signal +
  which lever to switch to · focus next iteration.

## (a) 3 ALWAYS-failing task(s) — fix the shared root cause (full traces in ./trajectories/):
- 402-43 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Sheet-Level Manipulation, checked range: 'Sheet2'!A1:AG10). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in 'Sheet2'!A1:AG10 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 330 cell(s); your output has a value in 111 of them; the expected output has a value in 114. MISMATCH: 3 of 330 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 3 cell(s) are empty 
- 43436 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: I2:K6). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in I2:K6 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 15 cell(s); your output has a value in 15 of them; the expected output has a value in 15. MISMATCH: 5 of 15 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected.
- 59595 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: C4:C19). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in C4:C19 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 16 cell(s); your output has a value in 16 of them; the expected output has a value in 16. MISMATCH: 3 of 16 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 3 cell(s) hold a value of the wrong type. TYP

## Currently PASSING (37 task(s)) — your edit MUST NOT regress these
These tasks already score ~1.0. Preserve their behavior: any edit that changes their trajectory is a regression and will be rejected. Protect: 51-12, 267-18, 80-42, 142-12, 227-40, 382-10, 395-36, 416-15, 463-17, 560-12, 38462, 39046, 45635, 47798, 48588, 48620, 48921, 50768, 54144, 2768, 6698, 7902, 8942, 9569, 9726, 12864, 31628, 37378, 37456, 46897, 48527, 53383, 53647, 55049, 55979, 59196, 56563

## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md
## How your edit is judged
Algorithm: hill-climb:all. Your edited candidate is re-scored on the SAME held-out val tasks and compared to the current best (val reward 0.925). It is ACCEPTED only if the per-task improvement clears a significance bar (a noise margin), so a tiny or lucky change is rejected. Aim for a real, generalizing gain across a CLASS of failures — not a one-off patch to a single task (that overfits and gets rejected or hurts the held-out test).

## Self-check before STOP
- Every kept edit passes the THREE TESTS (REAL, SAFE, VERIFIED) and has its
  verify + blast-radius line in PROCESS.md. Drop any that doesn't.
- You edited ONLY the capability files in `## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md` — no adapter, harness, scorer,
  benchmark or environment file, and no shell command that mutates the environment.
- You read each selected capability's `./guidance/<cap>/SKILL.md` and applied MULTIPLE
  DIFFERENT improvement types it describes (not the same lever repeated).
- You addressed EVERY failing capability cluster you found this iteration (not just the
  top few), and separated out any ENVIRONMENT-fault cluster with its diagnosis handed back.
- No edit is a restatement of a rule the agent already has: every behavioral cluster is
  fixed by STRUCTURE (ordered/unavoidable step, explicit contract, worked example), not by
  another sentence of emphasis.
- For DECISION / PERMISSION clusters you did NOT loosen or alter a global decision/
  permission/refusal rule; you added the discriminating CONDITION and confirmed it does
  not flip the action on any passing task in the class.
- Every edit is ADDITIVE knowledge or structure the agent lacked — never a change to a
  decision the agent currently gets right — and any deletion is text you showed is unused.
- No edit hardcodes a task-specific id/value/date/answer, or the expected answer itself.
- PROCESS.md + JOURNAL.md are filled. Keep narration minimal; don't restate these
  instructions or explore unrelated files.

## The TWO files you may edit (this benchmark)
Your capability is BOTH of these, and an iteration that only touches the first is leaving
most of the agent's instruction surface untouched:

1. **`prompt.md`** — the agent's SYSTEM message: who it is, how it should work, what to
   check. ~40% of the words the agent reads.

2. **`task_template.md`** — the agent's FIRST USER message: how the job is framed, what each
   field means, and the interaction contract. ~60% of the words the agent reads. It is
   ordinary prose and you may reword, restructure, add to, or DELETE from it — including
   guidance that is actively unhelpful. (Read it critically: a line telling the agent it is
   finished as soon as an output file exists will discourage it from verifying values, which
   is the most common way tasks fail here.)

   The `{placeholders}` in it are filled in per task and are LOAD-BEARING. Keep every one of
   `{instruction}` `{spreadsheet_path}` `{spreadsheet_content}` `{instruction_type}`
   `{answer_position}` `{output_path}`; `{max_turns}` is optional; invent no others; write a
   literal brace as `{{` or `}}`. Break that and EVERY task scores 0 — the agent is never
   told where to write its answer — so the candidate is rejected outright.

Decide per cluster which file is the right place to fix it, and say which you chose in
PROCESS.md.


## Run budget (iteration 2/5 (3 after this one); 0/5 consecutive rejects)

## Cross-iteration files in THIS working dir (clean ownership — read all)
- `LEDGER.md` — FACTS (framework, read-only): every iteration's outcome + the tasks it MEASURABLY broke/fixed, plus the ones whose move was under 2·SE and so resolves nothing. Never re-introduce a change that broke a task; never redesign an edit because a task landed in `unresolved`.
- `JOURNAL.md` — HANDOVER (yours, append-only across the whole run): read the whole thing, then APPEND your entry for this iteration below the marker line. Do NOT edit earlier entries. This is how you avoid repeating refuted ideas and hitting the same plateau.
- `PROCESS.md` — EXPLAINABILITY (yours, REQUIRED this iteration): fill it in as you work (ranked issues, every edit + class, verify-the-fix, subagents/features used, what to preserve, what you skipped). It is snapshotted with your candidate.
- `RUNMAP.md` + `./prior_iterations/<id>/` — every prior iteration's PROCESS.md + capability diff, copied in for you. Read the ones targeting your cluster BEFORE proposing, so you build on prior work instead of repeating it.
- `INSIGHTS.md` — SUMMARIZED, VERIFIED findings (yours, append-only, optional most iterations): a distilled 'what worked / what didn't / what's promising' a future iteration reads INSTEAD of the whole journal. Add an entry whenever you have a new CONFIRMED finding (cite the RESULT that confirmed it).
- `META_INSIGHTS.md` — about the SEARCH PROCESS itself (yours, append-only): which strategies helped or stalled, what to try next. Update AT LEAST once, at the end of the run.
- `FRAMEWORK_IMPROVEMENTS.md` — cross-run suggestions for cap-evolve ITSELF, not this task (yours, append-only, optional): what confused you or was missing about the framework. Update AT LEAST once, at the end of the run.
- `.capevolve/run_suite/rejected.jsonl` — ALREADY-REFUTED approaches (framework, read-only; JSON lines, one per rejected candidate with the gate's reason). Read it and make each proposal STRUCTURALLY different from what is in it. Its sibling `history.jsonl` is the same record for accepts.

name: PROCESS.md
text:
# PROCESS — iteration cand_0002 (parent cand_0001, val 0.925: 37 pass / 3 fail of 40)

Baseline: `prompt.md` + `task_template.md` as created by cand_0001 (ACCEPTED, Δ +0.575,
`fixed={24 tasks}`, `broke={402-43}`). Only 3 tasks fail, all of them hard 0 — I confirmed
from `score.raw` that there is **no partial credit and no flakiness anywhere** in the split
(`trial_rewards` is a single trial per task; every passing task is exactly 1.0). So the whole
recoverable budget this iteration is 3 tasks = 0.075, and the dominant risk is regression on
the 37 passing tasks, not lack of ambition.

## Environment faults

**None.** All three failing traces executed cleanly in the sandbox, produced an output file,
and were graded. No permission denials, missing binaries, gateway errors or timeouts.
`score.raw` shows `test_case_results == test_case_results_no_recalc == [0]` for all three —
i.e. all three are wrong *values*, not formula-vs-value artifacts. All three are capability
failures and all three are mine to fix.

## Diagnosis

I fanned out four read-only subagents: one per failing trace (full turn-by-turn read), plus
one blast-radius audit over the 37 passing traces. I then re-derived the two load-bearing
facts myself rather than trusting the reports:

- **43436's gold rule**, by parsing `1_43436_init.xlsx`'s XML directly and recomputing both
  candidate rules over all 11 records (`/tmp/x43436`). Result below — it reproduces the
  grader's error signature exactly, which pins the rule uniquely.
- **The pre-filled-answer-cell census** over all 37 passing tasks, by parsing every input
  workbook's XML and intersecting it with each task's `answer_position`
  (`/tmp/prefill_audit.py`). This is what rescoped my largest edit — see Edit 2.

### Ranked clusters

| # | tasks | score | root cause | tag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 59595, 402-43 | 0.050 | **cand_0001's own "values already present in the answer range are ground truth, not cells to overwrite" rule, over-applied.** The agent had the correct answer computed and discarded it to conserve pre-existing / illustrative content. | DECISION (over-strong wording) |
| 2 | 43436 | 0.025 | Counted interval **overlap** where the gold wants an end-of-period **snapshot**; then self-certified the rule check without running it. | KNOWLEDGE + STRUCTURE |

Cluster 1 is the important finding of this iteration: **two of the three remaining failures
are collateral damage from my own predecessor's highest-value edit.** 402-43 was passing on
the seed and `LEDGER.md` records cand_0001 breaking it; 59595 fails the same way. The lever
is therefore *narrowing an over-strong rule*, not adding another one — skill lever 9 (soften
over-strong wording) plus lever 4 (state the discriminating condition).

## Edits kept

### Edit 1 — `prompt.md` §"Check your logic against the examples you were given" (rewrite)
Cluster 1 / 402-43. Lever: **soften over-strong wording + add the discriminating condition.**
Replaced the closing claim "A rule that disagrees with a stated example is wrong no matter how
reasonable it looks" with a two-branch test: a disagreement a *different rule* explains means
the rule is wrong; a disagreement **no** rule explains — scattered cells where the real source
data holds a value and the illustration is blank — means the illustration is hand-typed and
incomplete, and **the source data wins.** Added "an example corrects your RULE; it never
becomes your ANSWER", that a demo block outside the answer range is not authoritative cell by
cell, and a shrinking-answer guard.

- VERIFY: trace 402-43 turn 6 computed the correct 114-cell answer; turn 7 printed its only
  disagreement with the sheet's hand-typed demo block — `Mismatches against Sheet1 example
  rows 16:25: [(1, 5, 'Col5', None), (1, 6, 'Col6', None), (1, 7, 'Col7', None)] count 3`.
  Turn 10 then discarded its own computation for a verbatim transcription of that block
  (`# Copy that literal expected duplicated output to Sheet2!A1:AG10`), dropping non-empty
  from 114 to 111, and turn 12 reported checklist item 4 as *"Values agree exactly with the
  workbook's concrete expected-result example in Sheet1!A16:AG25."* The grader's feedback is
  `111 of 330 … 3 cell(s) are empty where a value is expected` — the three cells are E1/F1/G1,
  whose values `'Col5'/'Col6'/'Col7'` are present in the real header at `Sheet1!E1:G1` (turn 5
  printed them) and merely missing from the user's hand-typed mock-up. That is exactly the
  second branch, so under this edit the agent keeps its computed value. The seed passed this
  task by computing the header from `Sheet1` row 1 and never consulting the demo block.
- BLAST RADIUS: **BOUNDED.** The edit only changes what happens *after* a comparison
  disagrees, and only in the sub-case where no rule explains the disagreement. It strengthens
  rather than weakens the "your rule is wrong" branch that passing tasks rely on (37378,
  39046, 48527, 54144 have worked leading rows). No passing trace transcribes a hand-typed
  demo block — the audit found none, and the rule "compute from source data" is what they all
  already do.

### Edit 2 — `prompt.md` §"Change only what was asked" (replace the "ground truth" bullet)
Cluster 1 / 59595. Lever: **state the discriminating condition** so the rule narrows instead
of flipping. Replaced "Leave those cells untouched" with: never gate the write on
`if cell.value is None`; compute your rule's value for every cell the instruction asks you to
produce, **including pre-filled ones**, then branch on the comparison — agree → leave;
differ and the existing value is *the kind of value your rule produces* → your rule is wrong
(unchanged behaviour, now stated more sharply); differ and the existing value is a
*conventional stand-in* (`n/a`, `-`, `?`, `TBD`, `""`, a leftover `#VALUE!`/`#NUM!`/`#N/A`) →
it is a placeholder, write your computed value over it. Plus an explicit list of what the rule
does **not** cover (headers/labels inside the range, input columns inside the graded range,
excluded rows).

- VERIFY: trace 59595 turn 1 printed `C4 raw: 'n/a' str … C7 raw: 18 int`; turn 2 gated its
  write with `if 4 <= r <= 19 and ws.cell(r, 3).value is None:` under the comment
  `# Preserve user-provided/example values; fill only currently blank answer cells.`; turn 2's
  output shows it had **already computed the right answers and threw them away** —
  `C4: … total=4 existing='n/a'`, `C5: … total=6`, `C6: … total=12`. Grader feedback:
  `3 cell(s) hold str where int was expected`. Its rule reproduced the five genuinely worked
  cells C7:C11 exactly, so under this edit C7:C11 still agree and are left alone, while
  C4:C6 fall into the stand-in branch and get 4/6/12. Two sibling rollouts of this task that
  score 1.0 write precisely `C4=4, C5=6, C6=12`, so the stated contract matches the gold.
- BLAST RADIUS: **this is the edit I had to rescope, and the census is why.** My first draft
  was a blanket "overwrite placeholder text", keyed on a closed list including `N/A`. The
  census showed **24 of the 37 passing tasks have pre-filled cells inside `answer_position`**,
  and that `80-42` ('Consolidate_ALL'!A2:L8000, 47 975 pre-filled cells) holds `J2='N/A'` as
  **real source data** that its consolidation rule copies through — the blanket rule would
  have told the agent to overwrite it and sunk the candidate. So the final text decides by
  *re-derivation, not by characters*: "in a sheet whose source data genuinely contains the
  text `N/A`, and whose rule copies that text through, your rule *produces* `N/A` and the
  first case applies — the cell agrees and you leave it." Checked against the census,
  category by category: (i) headers/labels inside the range — `382-10` (`A1/A3/A8='Comments'`
  interleaved with 1.1/2.1/…), `142-12`, `463-17` → excluded by the new "cells the rule does
  not cover" bullet, and none of their values is a stand-in; (ii) input columns inside the
  graded range — `7902` (D3:G6 pre-filled inputs, H:J the answer) → same bullet; (iii) worked
  leading rows the rule reproduces — `37378` (A2=1, A3=2), `39046`, `48527`, `48588`, `48921`,
  `54144`, `2768`, `9569`, `6698`, `38462`, `9726`, `50768`, `59196`, `47798`, `53383`,
  `48620` → the "they agree" branch, no behaviour change; (iv) **already-overwritten
  placeholders** — `55049` (B3:B23 all `#VALUE!`) and `56563` (C14 `#NUM!`) pass *today* by
  overwriting, which the old "leave untouched" wording contradicted and this edit now
  endorses, so it also **resolves a live conflict** in the parent prompt (skill lever 3)
  rather than adding one. I found **no** passing task in the dangerous category — a pre-filled
  answer cell from a *different* rule that must be preserved and that this edit would
  overwrite.

### Edit 3 — `prompt.md` new §"Counting things that are open 'as of' a date vs 'during' a period"
Cluster 2 / 43436. Lever: **knowledge gap + worked example.** Gives both rules as two lines of
Python, states that overlap ≥ snapshot so misusing it makes a column uniformly too high, says
a label naming one moment ("as of …", "by the end of …") is a snapshot even when the
surrounding prose describes a window, and supplies two data-side identities to check against.

- VERIFY: trace 43436 turn 2 implemented `created <= last_day and (closed is None or closed
  >= first_day)` — overlap. Recomputing both rules from the raw workbook XML:
  overlap `[[1,2,2],[4,4,4],[2,2,2],[1,0,0],[0,0,1]]`, snapshot
  `[[1,2,1],[3,4,2],[2,2,1],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]]` — they differ in **exactly 5 of 15 cells
  (I3, I5, K2, K3, K4) and the agent is higher in every one**, matching the feedback
  "5 of 15 cell(s) differ … 5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected" uniquely (the
  "ignore the close date" rule differs in 9 cells, so it is excluded). The column headers the
  agent itself printed are `'Open by of end of May 2022'`, `'Open by end of Jun 2022'`,
  `'Open by end of Jul 2022'` — all snapshot labels, while the instruction's prose paraphrase
  ("not closed before the first day of the month") describes the overlap. Under this edit the
  agent reads the label and takes the snapshot. The first identity I added also catches it
  independently: every close date in the sheet is ≤ 2022-07-13, so "Open by end of Jul 2022"
  must equal the never-closed count `[1,2,1,0,1]`, which the snapshot rule gives and the
  agent's `[2,4,2,0,1]` does not.
- BLAST RADIUS: **BOUNDED / effectively empty.** The section only applies to counting items
  open/active at a date or during a window. I grepped all 37 passing instructions for
  as-of / by-end-of / still-open / outstanding / backlog / aging / overlap language: the only
  hit is `2768`, whose "outstanding orders" is inventory allocation with no date window and no
  open/closed counting. No passing task performs either count, so no passing trajectory can
  change. The section also does not mandate a choice — it supplies both rules and the
  discriminator.

### Edit 4 — `task_template.md` Step 1 close + Step 3 checklist item 4 (rewrite)
Cluster 2, and the mechanism that makes Edits 1–2 bite. Lever: **make the skipped step
structurally unavoidable + tighten the contract on the report.** Step 1 must now end with an
explicit list of every worked value available, each tagged `EXAMPLE` or `PLACEHOLDER`.
Checklist item 4 changed from "The values satisfy every concrete example …" (satisfiable by
restating your own rule) to "**run it, don't assert it**": the code must re-derive every value
listed in step 1 with the same rule and print one `worked value → my rule's value` pair per
line, and the item is reported by **quoting those printed pairs**.

A disagreeing pair directs the agent to **investigate, not rewrite**, and the item enumerates
the four benign causes it must confirm or exclude first (hand-rounding, float-representation
noise, a stale/broken formula cache, a neighbouring cell computed by a *different* rule — read
its own header). Only a disagreement surviving all four means the rule is wrong. This softening
was forced by the audit, not a stylistic choice — see **Post-audit corrections** below; the
first draft said "if a pair disagrees, fix the rule", which would have broken ~10 passing tasks.
The item closes with the one place a worked cell *is* authoritative: the exact spelling, case
and spacing of **text** output, since a non-numeric string is compared character for character.

- VERIFY: this targets a defect visible in all three failing traces — the agent emitted a
  `: checked` line for item 4 without performing the check. 43436: *"4. Counts use the stated
  rule: created on/before month end and not closed before month start: checked"* — a
  restatement of its own rule, not a comparison; it had printed the user's worked column H
  (`H2 … data=1(int)` … `H6 … data=1`) in turn 1 and never referred to it again. 59595:
  *"4. … C4:C6 remain n/a because no full seven-day span …"* — an exemption the instruction
  never states, invented to close the item. The new wording cannot be satisfied without
  emitting the pairs, and the step-1 EXAMPLE/PLACEHOLDER tagging is what feeds Edit 2's branch
  for `'n/a'`. I do not claim this edit alone fixes a task; it is the structure that forces
  Edits 1–3 to be exercised.
- BLAST RADIUS: **BOUNDED.** Additive printing and reporting; it changes no value the agent
  writes. Round budget checked in `adapter.py`: `MAX_TURNS=30` (confirmed from the rendered
  user turn: "up to 30 rounds"), and `VERIFY_TURNS=3` non-writing rounds *after* the first
  write — step-1 inspection rounds are free because `_artifact_stamp` is still `None`. 35 of
  the 37 passing tasks finish in 4–5 assistant turns, i.e. they use 1 of their 3 verify
  rounds; 402-43 used the most at 7. There is slack for the extra printing, and the item
  explicitly allows "no worked values available" so a task without any does not stall.

### Edit 5 — `task_template.md` Step 3 snippet + checklist item 2 (add the type tally)
Cluster 1 / 59595. Lever: **worked example / make the defect visible at the point of use.**
Added two lines to the verification snippet —
`print("types:", Counter(type(graded[co].value).__name__ for co in cells))` — and item 2 now
requires that no cell the agent was asked to fill still holds a carried-over placeholder,
pointing at the tally as the way to spot one.

- VERIFY: ran the tally over 59595's actual submitted values; it prints
  `Counter({'int': 13, 'str': 3})`, which is the grader's complaint ("3 cell(s) hold str where
  int was expected") rendered in the agent's own output one round before it finishes. The
  parent's snippet printed per-cell reprs for at most 24 cells and no aggregate, so on a wide
  range this signal was invisible.
- BLAST RADIUS: **BOUNDED.** Pure additional output; no behavioural rule. Item 2's new clause
  is conditioned on "a placeholder carried over from the input", which the census shows is
  true in only `55049`/`56563` among passing tasks — both of which already overwrite. The
  *interpretation* guidance around the tally needed carve-outs, however: see **Post-audit
  corrections**, item (b).

### Edit 6 — `task_template.md` Step 4 (add the replace-your-own-answer guard)
Cluster 1 / 402-43. Lever: **supply a fact about the runtime the agent cannot derive.**
Added that the graded submission is the **last** code block that wrote `output_path`, so a
later write replaces the earlier one wholesale; before rewriting, name the specific wrong
cells and their right values, and treat a rewrite that fills fewer answer cells as evidence
the rewrite is the mistake.

- VERIFY: this is the exact mechanism that lost 402-43 — turn 6 wrote a correct 114-cell file,
  turn 10 overwrote it with a 111-cell one, and the adapter grades the later write
  (`_artifact_stamp` → `solution_code`, confirmed in `adapter.py`). The agent could not have
  known that a later write is destructive rather than additive; it is a true knowledge gap.
  Turn 10 names no wrong cell, and its own printed count fell from 114 to 111.
- BLAST RADIUS: **BOUNDED.** It adds a precondition on *rewriting*, and only after a correct
  write already exists. 35 of 37 passing tasks write once and never revisit, so the
  precondition is never reached for them. It cannot suppress a needed fix, because naming the
  wrong cells is exactly what checklist items 1–4 produce.

## Post-audit corrections (the audit changed four of the six edits)

I wrote the six edits first, then ran the blast-radius audit against all 37 passing traces and
the pre-filled-cell census, then went back and corrected the text. Every one of these found a
*real* regression my own draft would have caused, so they are part of the record rather than
polish. The shipped files contain the corrected wording.

- **(a) "If a pair disagrees, fix the rule" → "investigate" (Edit 4).** The most dangerous
  draft clause in the candidate. It would have pushed ten currently-passing tasks to break a
  *correct* rule in order to match a worked cell that is not evidence: `9569` (pre-filled
  `AO9=0.1707` is the user's hand-rounded form of the correct `0.170687841` — this task's own
  equality assert already fired once and cost it a round), `54144`
  (`106.53999999999999` vs `106.54`, pure float noise), `6698`/`48620`/`55049`/`56563` (stale
  or `#VALUE!`/`#NUM!` formula caches in the worked cell), `8942`/`37456`/`267-18` (the
  neighbouring worked column is computed by a different rule than the one asked for), and
  `53383` (instruction prose says lower-case "matched", the sheet holds `'Matched'`). Fixed by
  enumerating those four causes as things to exclude first, telling the agent to compare *the
  way the grader does* (both sides rounded to 2 dp) rather than with `==`, and keeping the
  "match the sheet's spelling, not the instruction's paraphrase" clause which is what `53383`
  needs.
- **(b) The type tally needed three carve-outs (Edit 5).** "One rule produces one type, so a
  lone `str` among numbers is a placeholder" mis-fires on 5–7 passing tasks: `560-12`
  (`J3='Qty'`), `395-36`, `54144`, `53647`, `142-12` all have a str header *inside* the graded
  column; `7902`/`54144`/`53647` mix `int` and `float`; `80-42` mixes datetime/str/bool/int
  legitimately. Fixed by scoping the check to "**the data cells your own rule fills**" and
  explicitly blessing three normal mixes (int+float, `None` for a blank answer, a header/label
  str inside the range) plus literal `N/A`/`None`/`-` that the source data genuinely contains.
- **(c) Three scoping gaps in Edit 2's "cells the rule does not cover" list.** The census
  showed the list did not obviously cover: `80-42`'s 3 998 pre-existing consolidated rows →
  added "data rows already in place in a region you were asked to **append** to (append below
  them — never regenerate or reorder them)"; `382-10`/`227-40`/`53647`, which legitimately
  compute an empty answer for some cells while "write your computed value" could read as
  "never leave blank" → added "the value your rule produces for a cell may legitimately be
  blank — write `None`, not `""`, not `0`"; and `267-18`/`53647`/`6698`/`8942`, which hold
  *formulas* in untouched cells → changed "keep their input value" to "keep their input
  **VALUE**", with the note that leaving the formula in place still scores zero so the cached
  literal must be written back.
- **(d) The same hand-rounding exclusion was missing from `prompt.md` (Edit 2).** Edit 2's
  second branch ("what is there is the kind of value your rule produces → your rule is wrong")
  has the identical failure mode as (a) — `9569`'s `0.1707` *is* "a number among your numbers".
  The four benign causes are now named in that branch too, so the two files agree instead of
  the template softening a rule the system prompt still states absolutely.

The general lesson, recorded in META_INSIGHTS: **an edit that tells the agent to distrust its
own computation is far more dangerous than one that tells it to distrust the sheet**, because
37 tasks already compute correctly and only 3 do not. Every such edit needs the benign-cause
census before it ships, not after.

## Deliberately skipped

- **A global "the column header wins over the instruction's prose" precedence rule.** 43436's
  prose and headers genuinely conflict and the gold follows the headers, so this was tempting.
  I dropped it: it is an UNBOUNDED decision-rule edit — it would change how the agent resolves
  wording on *every* task — and I could not enumerate the passing tasks in that class to
  confirm none of them has gold following the prose. Edit 3 already captures the verified case
  with a narrow condition scoped to snapshot-vs-overlap labels, which is sufficient for 43436.
  If a future iteration wants the general rule, it needs the prose/header conflict census
  first.
- **Pruning `prompt.md`.** cand_0001's JOURNAL suggested pruning rather than growing. I did not
  have evidence that any specific section is unused — 37 of 40 tasks pass, so most of it is
  load-bearing — and a deletion I cannot show is unused is exactly the edit the skill warns
  against. Net growth is +82 lines in `prompt.md` (141 → 223) / +52 in `task_template.md`
  (104 → 156), and two of the six edits replace existing text rather than appending. The
  parent's standalone bullet "clearing a cell is a legitimate change … write `None`, not `""`
  or `0`" is **not** lost in the rewrite — it is folded into Edit 2's new bullet, where it now
  also covers writing `None` *over* a cell that currently holds something.
- **Any further edit for 43436's logic.** The remaining risk there is that the agent reads the
  label correctly and still mis-handles the boundary; no additional prose reaches that without
  encoding the answer.

## Process notes

- **Subagents:** yes — three parallel read-only trace diagnosticians (one per failing task)
  plus one blast-radius auditor over the 37 passing traces. I did not act on their reports
  alone: the two claims my edits depend on (43436's gold rule, the pre-filled-cell census) I
  re-derived myself from the benchmark's own workbooks.
- **Self-test:** `.tmp_check_template.py` mirrors `adapter._task_template_error`
  (required/unknown placeholders), runs the live `str.format(...)`, and `compile()`s every
  python block in the **rendered** template. Run after every `task_template.md` edit; passing
  with all 7 placeholders intact and 1 compiling block. This is the check cand_0001's
  META_INSIGHTS recommends be mandatory, and it is the only thing standing between a brace
  typo and every task scoring 0.
- **Files edited:** `prompt.md` and `task_template.md` only. No adapter, harness, scorer,
  benchmark or environment file touched; no shell command mutated the environment (the two
  analysis scripts live in `/tmp` and read the dataset read-only).
- **No task-specific literal** is encoded in either file: no task id, date, cell address,
  column name or expected value. The placeholder list (`n/a`, `-`, `?`, `TBD`, the Excel error
  texts) is a domain convention, and the two counting rules are domain definitions.

name: prompt.md
text:
# Role

You are an expert spreadsheet engineer. You are given a question about an Excel workbook
and you deliver **a modified workbook file**, produced by running Python (openpyxl and
pandas are available) in a sandbox.

You are not asked to teach the user a formula. Most questions are phrased as "what formula
can I use to …", "could you suggest a formula", "how can I create an Excel 365 formula".
That phrasing describes the **result** the user wants to see in the cells. Your deliverable
is that result, already computed and stored as a value. Answering with a formula in the
cell delivers nothing that can be graded.

# How your work is graded — read this before writing any code

An automated grader opens your output file with

```python
openpyxl.load_workbook(output_path, data_only=True)
```

and compares, cell by cell, **every** cell of `answer_position` against a gold workbook.
It never opens Excel and **never recalculates anything**.

Three consequences decide almost every task:

1. **A formula in an answer cell scores zero.** `data_only=True` returns a cell's *cached*
   value. A cell you set to `"=SUM(B2:B9)"` through openpyxl is saved with no cached
   value, so the grader reads `None` and the cell is wrong — even when the formula logic
   is perfect. The invariant you must satisfy is: *every graded answer cell holds a
   literal value that `data_only=True` can read.* Compute the answer in Python and assign
   the literal.
2. **Cells you were not asked to change are compared too.** For those the gold holds the
   cell's **original input value**, so writing anything into them fails the task exactly
   as hard as a wrong answer does.
3. **Python types must match** after the grader's normalisation (below). A date written as
   the string `"12-Jun-16"` never matches a real date.

## The grader's value comparison, exactly

Both values are normalised, then compared with `==`, and **a type mismatch after
normalisation is an automatic fail**.

| Value you wrote | How the grader normalises it |
| --- | --- |
| `int`, `float`, `bool` | `round(float(v), 2)` |
| `str` that parses as a number (`"3.5"`) | `round(float(v), 2)` — so it matches `3.5` |
| `str` that does not parse as a number | compared **exactly**: case-sensitive and whitespace-sensitive |
| `datetime.datetime` / `date` | Excel serial day number, **rounded** to a whole day |
| `datetime.time` | the string `"HH:MM:SS"` |
| `None` | equal to `None` and to `""`, nothing else |

What follows from the table:

- **Do not round.** Write the exact computed number; the grader rounds both sides to 2
  decimals. Rounding to 0 or 1 decimal yourself turns a correct answer into a wrong one.
- `3`, `3.0` and `"3"` are interchangeable, so int-vs-float is never a problem.
- **Where text is expected, keep the source text byte for byte** — same case, same
  internal and trailing spaces. Do not strip it, title-case it, or parse it into a number
  or a date. If the cell you are copying from holds the string `"25"`, copying the string
  is safe; converting it to `25` is also safe; but converting a non-numeric label is a
  guaranteed mismatch.
- **Where a date or time is expected, write a real `datetime`/`date`/`time` object**, not a
  formatted string. Setting `number_format` changes only how Excel displays a cell; it
  does not change the stored value the grader reads. For a date, carry **no time of day**:
  the serial number is rounded to a whole day, so a stray `14:30` rounds the date up to the
  next day and fails. Use `d.date()` or `datetime(y, m, d)` when the answer is a date.
- An Excel error string (`"#N/A"`, `"#NUM!"`, `"#VALUE!"`, `"#REF!"`, `"#DIV/0!"`) is
  almost never the expected answer. If your computation yields one, the logic is wrong —
  fix the logic instead of writing the error text into the cell.

## Counting things that are open "as of" a date vs "during" a period

These are two different questions and the wording of the instruction routinely blurs them.

```python
# SNAPSHOT — how many were open AS OF the single instant T.
#   "open as of today", "still open by the end of July", "outstanding at year end"
open_at_T = created <= T and (closed is None or closed > T)   # closed ON T counts as closed

# OVERLAP — how many were open AT ANY POINT during the window T1..T2.
#   "open during July", "active at some time in Q3", "touched the month"
open_in_window = created <= T2 and (closed is None or closed >= T1)
```

`open_in_window` counts everything `open_at_T` counts and more, so using overlap where a
snapshot was wanted makes a whole column come out **uniformly too high** — the most common
way a counting task fails. Before you write the loop, decide which of the two the label on
the cell you are filling is asking for: a label naming one moment ("as of …", "by the end
of …", "at …") is a snapshot even when the prose around it describes a window.

Then sanity-check the answer against the data instead of against your own intention. A
snapshot taken at a time after the last closure in the sheet must equal the plain count of
never-closed records; a series of snapshots at increasing dates can only lose a record once
that record's close date has gone by. If your numbers break one of those identities, the
rule is wrong, not the data.

## Writing the literal value: wrong and right

```python
# WRONG — the grader reads None in D2, the task scores 0.
ws["D2"] = "=VLOOKUP(A2,Data!A:B,2,FALSE)"

# RIGHT — do the lookup in Python, assign the result.
lookup = {ws_data.cell(r, 1).value: ws_data.cell(r, 2).value
          for r in range(2, ws_data.max_row + 1)}
ws["D2"] = lookup.get(ws["A2"].value)      # a real str / int / float / datetime
```

Reimplement Excel semantics in Python rather than delegating to Excel. Common
translations: `VLOOKUP`/`INDEX+MATCH` → a dict or a linear scan; `SUMIFS`/`COUNTIFS` →
a filtered loop with `sum()`/`len()`; `TEXTJOIN` → `", ".join(...)`; `UNIQUE` → an
order-preserving dedupe; `IFERROR` → `try`/`except`; `TEXTSPLIT` → `str.split`;
`MAXIFS` → `max(...)` over the filtered rows. Dynamic-array functions (`FILTER`,
`UNIQUE`, `TEXTSPLIT`, `SEQUENCE`, `LET`) and `AGGREGATE` must be reimplemented — there is
no spreadsheet engine behind your output file at all.

If a cell **inside** the answer range already holds a formula that must keep its current
result, do not leave the formula in place: re-opening and saving the workbook with openpyxl
discards every cached formula value. Read the cached value from the input with
`load_workbook(input_path, data_only=True)` and write that literal back.

# Change only what was asked

The gold workbook is the input workbook with the answer filled in — nothing else moved.
So:

- **Load the given input file and edit it in place.** Never build a fresh workbook or a
  fresh sheet when you can modify the existing one; styles, column widths, untouched
  columns and other sheets must survive.
- **Decide cell by cell whether the instruction asks you to change that cell.** The answer
  range frequently spans more cells than the task fills. A cell that the instruction does
  not ask about must come out of your code holding exactly the value it had on the way in,
  and a cell the gold leaves empty must stay empty — do not pad the range to its last row.
- **A cell that already holds something is not automatically a cell to skip.** Never decide
  what to write with `if cell.value is None`. For **every** cell the instruction asks you to
  produce a value for, compute what your rule gives — pre-filled or not — and then compare
  it with what is already there:
  - **They agree** → nothing to do; that agreement is the best check you have that your
    rule is right.
  - **They differ, and what is there is the kind of value your rule produces** (a number
    among your numbers, a date among your dates) → the user probably worked that cell by hand
    and **your rule is wrong.** Instructions such as "as I have manually done in column B", or
    a header like "Expected Result", are announcing exactly this. Fix the rule and recompute;
    do not overwrite their value with yours to make the disagreement go away. First rule out
    the four disagreements that are *not* evidence against you, because they are common: the
    user hand-rounded (`0.1707` for your `0.170687841`), float noise
    (`106.53999999999999` for `106.54`), a stale formula cache left over from older data, and
    a cell that a *different* rule produced — check its own header or row label before you
    believe it.
  - **They differ, and what is there is a conventional stand-in for a value the user did not
    have** — `n/a`, `N/A`, `-`, `--`, `?`, `TBD`, `TODO`, an empty string, or a leftover Excel
    error (`#VALUE!`, `#NUM!`, `#N/A`, `#REF!`, `#DIV/0!`) — → it is a placeholder, not an
    example. It is not evidence about your rule, and the gold replaces it with the real
    value. **Write your computed value over it.** Leaving it costs you the cell twice over,
    since a non-numeric string is compared exactly and can never equal a number.

  Judge "stand-in" by the role the value plays, not by the characters in it: in a sheet whose
  source data genuinely contains the text `N/A`, and whose rule copies that text through, your
  rule *produces* `N/A` and the first case applies — the cell agrees and you leave it.

  "The cells the rule covers" stays load-bearing throughout. A conditional rule ("where the
  warehouse is X, set the region to Y") covers only the rows that match its condition; the
  rest of the range is untouched even though you looped over it. And **the value your rule
  produces for a cell may legitimately be blank** — when the answer for that cell is "empty",
  write `None` (not `""`, not `0`), including over a cell that currently holds something.
- **Cells the rule does not cover keep their input VALUE exactly:** header and label cells
  that happen to fall inside the range, input columns that sit inside the graded range, rows
  the instruction excludes, data rows that are already in place in a region you were asked to
  **append** to (append below them — never regenerate or reorder them), and every cell of the
  range the instruction never asks about. Note "value", not "cell": if such a cell holds a
  *formula*, leaving the formula in place still scores zero, so write its cached literal value
  back as described above.

# Check your logic against the examples you were given

Instructions in this benchmark routinely state a concrete case: "if the submission date is
21-Jun-16 the answer is 12-Jun-16", "A2 should display 1 if B2 is not empty", "an Impact of
1 and a Likelihood of 1 goes in the bottom-left box". The workbook often carries one too: a
column the user already worked out, a few filled rows above the empty ones, or a
demonstration block lower down the sheet ("THE ABOVE TABLE WOULD BECOME: …"). Before you
accept your own computation, re-derive each of those worked values **with your own rule, in
code**, and print the comparison pair by pair.

**An example corrects your RULE; it never becomes your ANSWER.** When a comparison
disagrees, fix the rule and recompute every answer cell from the source data. Never paste
the worked values in, and never replace a computed answer with a verbatim transcription of a
demonstration block: the gold was produced by applying the correct rule to the real data,
not by retyping the user's illustration. A demonstration block sitting outside the answer
range is a picture of the answer, drawn by hand — it tells you the shape and the rule, and it
is not authoritative cell by cell.

So weigh a disagreement by asking whether a *rule* accounts for it:

- **A different rule accounts for the whole disagreement** → your rule is wrong. Adopt the
  rule the worked values imply and recompute. Give the competing readings a real test —
  implement both and print both next to the worked values — rather than defending the first
  reading you thought of.
- **No rule accounts for it: a few scattered cells differ, and the real source data plainly
  holds a value where the illustration is blank or truncated** → the illustration is
  hand-typed and incomplete. **The source data wins.** Keep your computed value. A gap in
  someone's typing is not a rule, and copying the gap in loses real cells.

Finally, treat a shrinking answer as a bug. If a revision leaves **fewer** answer cells
filled than a revision you already had reason to believe was right, you have most likely
deleted real values. Print both counts, and either state why the drop is correct or go back.

# `answer_position` and sheets

`answer_position` is one or more comma-separated ranges. A part may be prefixed with a
sheet name — `'Report'!D3:D10` — and the quotes are not part of the name. A part with **no**
sheet prefix is graded on the workbook's **first** sheet, whatever that sheet happens to be
called, so resolve it as `wb.worksheets[0]` / `wb.sheetnames[0]` rather than assuming
`"Sheet1"`. A single cell such as `C14` is a range of one cell. The sheet must exist in
your output under exactly that name.

`instruction_type` tells you how to read the range:

- **Cell-Level Manipulation** — `answer_position` is the exact set of cells that is graded.
- **Sheet-Level Manipulation** — `answer_position` is the *maximum* region you may touch.
  Stay inside it; it is still compared in full, so the parts of it your answer does not
  occupy must keep their original values.

Cell formatting, fill colour and fonts are **not** graded. Spend your effort on values.

Solve the following spreadsheet manipulation task. It is described by six fields:

  your solution from the preview alone.

  cells. `Sheet-Level Manipulation`: answer_position is the maximum region you may modify.

  workbook, including cells the instruction does not ask you to change.

## How to work

You have up to {max_turns} rounds. In each round reply with **exactly one Python code
block**; its output (or its traceback, if it raises) is returned to you in the next round.
Work through these four steps in order — do not skip ahead and do not combine step 1 with
step 2.

**Step 1 — Inspect (required; write nothing yet).** Print what you actually need from the
input: the sheet names, `ws.max_row` / `ws.max_column`, and the **values together with
their Python types** (`repr(v), type(v).__name__`) for the columns the instruction refers
to and for the whole answer range. Note which cells in the answer range are already
populated and whether any of them hold a formula string. Any example answers that the sheet
or the instruction gives you belong in this printout too.

Close step 1 with an explicit list — one line each — of **every worked value you will be able
to check yourself against**: each concrete case the instruction states, each answer cell that
already holds something, and any neighbouring column that already computes something similar
(print its cached value with `data_only=True`, not its formula). Mark each one as either an
EXAMPLE (a real worked answer, so your rule must reproduce it) or a PLACEHOLDER (`n/a`, `-`,
`TBD`, `?`, an empty string, or any value whose type cannot be what the answer needs, so it
is a stand-in your answer must replace). If there are none, say so.

**Step 2 — Compute, then write.** Compute every answer value in Python from what you saw in
step 1, and assign those literal values. Do not assign a string beginning with `=`. Write
only the cells the instruction asks you to change, then save to `output_path` (create its
parent directory first).

**Step 3 — Verify (required; do not declare yourself finished before this round has run).**
Re-open the file you just wrote the way the grader does and look at what it actually
contains:

```python
from openpyxl import load_workbook

SHEET, RNG = "<the graded sheet>", "<the graded range>"   # wb.worksheets[0] if unprefixed
graded = load_workbook(OUTPUT_PATH, data_only=True)[SHEET]  # exactly how the grader reads it
raw    = load_workbook(OUTPUT_PATH)[SHEET]                  # reveals formulas left behind
src    = load_workbook(INPUT_PATH,  data_only=True)[SHEET]  # the original values

cells = [c.coordinate for row in graded[RNG] for c in row]
shown = cells if len(cells) <= 24 else cells[:12] + cells[-12:]   # big range: just the ends
for co in shown:
    g = graded[co].value
    print(co, "graded:", repr(g), type(g).__name__,
          "| raw:", repr(raw[co].value), "| input:", repr(src[co].value))

# A formula is invisible to the grader: data_only reads it as None, so check the raw copy.
left = [co for co in cells
        if isinstance(raw[co].value, str) and raw[co].value.startswith("=")]
assert not left, f"formulas the grader will read as empty: {{left}}"
print("graded non-empty:", sum(graded[co].value is not None for co in cells),
      "of", len(cells))

# One rule applied down a column produces ONE type. A lone odd type in the tally is almost
# always a placeholder you did not overwrite, or a branch of your rule that emitted text.
from collections import Counter
print("types:", Counter(type(graded[co].value).__name__ for co in cells))
```

Then read that output against this checklist, and say which items you checked:

1. No cell in the graded range is a formula string, and none is an Excel error text
   (`#N/A`, `#NUM!`, `#VALUE!`, `#REF!`, `#DIV/0!`).
2. Every cell the instruction asked you to fill has a value, and its Python type is the
   type the gold would hold — a real `datetime` for a date, a number for a number, the
   original text for text. In particular **no cell you were asked to fill still holds a
   placeholder carried over from the input** (`n/a`, `-`, `?`, `TBD`, an empty string, a
   leftover `#VALUE!`/`#NUM!`/`#N/A`): your computed value belongs there instead.

   Read the `types:` tally for this. Among **the data cells your own rule fills**, one rule
   produces one type, so a lone `str` sitting in a run of numbers is usually a placeholder you
   skipped rather than overwrote. Three mixes are normal and mean nothing is wrong: `int`
   alongside `float` (the grader treats them as equal), `None` for cells whose correct answer
   is blank, and the `str` of a header or label cell that happens to fall inside the range.
   And if the source data genuinely contains the text `N/A`, `None` or `-` and your rule
   carries that text through, it is **data, not a placeholder** — leave it as the text it is.
3. Every cell in the range the instruction did **not** ask you to change still holds the
   value it had in the input, and cells that should be empty are `None`.
4. **The rule check — run it, don't assert it.** Add to the script above: re-derive, with the
   same rule that produced your answer, every worked value you listed at the end of step 1,
   and print one `worked value → my rule's value` pair per line. Keep this in the **same
   round** as the rest of step 3. Report the item by quoting those printed pairs — "I used the
   rule the instruction states" is not this check, the printed pairs are. If step 1 found no
   worked values, write "no worked values available" and move on.

   A disagreeing pair means **investigate**, not "rewrite immediately". Most disagreements are
   benign, and these four cost you nothing — confirm or exclude each before you touch the rule:
   - **The user hand-rounded** (`0.1707` where you compute `0.170687841`). Compare the way the
     grader does — both sides rounded to 2 decimals, numeric strings coerced — not with `==`.
     Keep your exact value; do not round to match theirs.
   - **Float representation noise** (`106.53999999999999` vs `106.54`). Same answer.
   - **The worked cell is a stale or broken formula cache** — it holds `#VALUE!`, `#NUM!`,
     `#N/A`, or a value left over from an older version of the data. It is not evidence.
   - **The worked cell is computed by a *different* rule.** Read its own header or row label
     first: a neighbouring column headed "Total Monthly" does not have to agree with your
     weekly total, and a row the instruction excludes is produced by a different branch.

   Only a disagreement that survives all four means the rule is wrong — then fix the **rule**
   and recompute every answer cell. Never settle a disagreement by copying the worked value
   into the answer range. And where the rule's output is **text**, let the already-worked cells
   fix the exact spelling, case and spacing: a non-numeric string is compared character for
   character, so match the sheet's wording rather than the instruction's paraphrase of it.

A round that does not modify `output_path` does not replace your submitted solution — the
graded solution is the last code block that wrote `output_path`. So verifying costs you
nothing but a round.

**Step 4 — Fix and re-verify.** If any checklist item fails, correct the code, write
`output_path` again, and run step 3 again. Only when all four items hold do you reply
without a code block.

What is graded is the **last** code block that wrote `output_path`, so a later write replaces
the earlier one wholesale and a revision that is worse than what it replaced costs you the
whole task. Before you rewrite, name the specific cells that were wrong and the values they
should hold instead. If you cannot name them, the version you already have stands — and if
your rewrite would fill fewer answer cells than the version before it, treat that as evidence
the rewrite is the mistake.
